slides.title: From videos to a moving 3D scene
bullets: Goal: replay a skate trick from a new viewpoint.
Part 1: how the reconstruction works.
Part 2: data acquisition and actual results.
slides.notes: The goal of my project is to reconstruct a moving 3D scene from videos, so that I can choose a new viewpoint and a moment in the replay. I will first explain the reconstruction process, step by step. Then I will present the data acquisition and compare the kitchen reference scene with my own True Skate recordings.

slides.title: Step 1 — prepare images of the same moment
bullets: Extract frames from each camera view.
Align the moments represented by the frames.
Keep image size and camera parameters consistent.
slides.notes: The first step is to turn the videos into image sequences. At each training instant, the views should show the same state of the scene. Otherwise, the model receives conflicting observations. Image resizing must also be reflected in the camera parameters. In the project, FFmpeg extracts the frames and Python prepares the dataset. This uses the course concepts of sampling and image coordinates. Later, I will explain how I acquired the actual recordings.

slides.title: Step 2 — recover the cameras and 3D points
bullets: Find the same background details in several images.
Estimate camera poses and triangulate 3D points.
Check that the points project back to the right pixels.
slides.notes: The reconstruction needs the position and orientation of each camera, as well as its projection parameters. If these are not supplied, COLMAP estimates them from matching details in the static background. It estimates camera poses and triangulates sparse 3D points, then refines them together. Reprojection checks compare predicted pixels with observed pixels. This applies the course topics of coordinate transformations and perspective. For the kitchen dataset, calibrated cameras are supplied; for True Skate, I estimate them.

slides.title: Step 3 — learn a scene made of Gaussians
bullets: Start with 3D elements: position, size, rotation and opacity.
Project them into a camera to render an image.
Compare with the target and update the scene.
slides.notes: The scene is represented by many small 3D Gaussian elements, rather than a triangle mesh. Each element has a position, size, orientation, opacity and appearance. Starting from the initial points, the renderer projects and combines their contributions into pixels. Training compares this image with the recorded target and uses gradients to update the scene. Density control can add or remove elements. This connects perspective, visibility and rasterization. I reuse the authors' implementation and provide project scripts for preparation and validation.

slides.title: Step 4 — model motion and check the result
bullets: 4DGaussians predicts how the reference scene changes with time.
Dynamic 3D Gaussians fits successive states with motion constraints.
Render the scene and compare it with a reserved camera view.
slides.notes: To represent motion, the scene must change with time. Four-D Gaussians uses a shared deformation network. Dynamic Three-D Gaussians instead fits successive states with local motion constraints. Both receive calibrated cameras as input. After training, I request a time and viewpoint and compare the rendered image with a reserved camera view. The latest ten-time pilot uses all ten times for supervision, so it tests a reserved viewpoint, not unseen-time interpolation. Reliable rendering also does not automatically validate physical tracking.

slides.title: Two sources of data, two levels of control
bullets: Kitchen reference: synchronized videos and supplied calibration.
True Skate: one saved replay recorded from successive viewpoints.
Fixed views simplify calibration; timing and masks remain approximate.
slides.notes: I used two sources of data. First, I downloaded a kitchen scene from the DyNeRF reference dataset, with synchronized videos and supplied camera calibration. Second, I recorded the same saved True Skate replay from different viewpoints. I initially used following cameras, then captured fixed views to simplify pose estimation. The screen recording was split automatically and aligned using the score event. This is not a simultaneous physical camera rig. Exact replay timing, camera estimates and foreground masks still contain uncertainty.

slides.title: Kitchen reference: the pipeline works
bullets: A recognizable scene with reconstructed motion.
A small, calibrated reference experiment.
Blur and color differences remain.
slides.notes: This is the kitchen reference experiment. On the left is an input image. On the right is the actual trained model; the PowerPoint includes a three-second animation. The reconstruction is recognizable and changes with time, which confirms that the GPU pipeline can learn a dynamic scene on this calibrated input. This remains a small pilot of about one second, with blur and color errors. It is not a complete reconstruction or a physical tracking result.

slides.title: My recordings: the moving board is still difficult
slides.section: Part 2 / Own-data result and next steps
bullets: The background is recognizable, but board motion is unreliable.
Separate static fits work better at selected instants.
Next: check timing, masks and initially visible surfaces.
slides.notes: With my own recordings, the result is much less convincing. The background can be recognizable, but the moving board is blurred or missing. Independent static fits worked better at selected instants. My Dynamic Three-D Gaussians pilot also lost the board after a good initial fit. Timing, masks, camera uncertainty and surface visibility are hypotheses to investigate, not proven individual causes. The kitchen and skate experiments also have different scenes and settings. My next priority is to improve and check the inputs before making a reliable motion or rotation claim.

slides.title: Code example: project 3D points into pixels
bullets: 1. Transform world points into the camera frame.
2. Divide by depth to apply perspective.
3. Convert the result to pixel coordinates.
slides.notes: This is the project function, with spacing expanded for readability. Points contains 3D coordinates. Pose contains the camera rotation and translation. Multiplication and translation produce camera coordinates. Dividing the first two coordinates by depth applies perspective. The focal length scales the result and the principal point offsets it into the image. The function also returns depth for visibility checks.

slides.title: Code example: protect the validation images
bullets: A foreground mask can guide training.
A validation mask must only evaluate the result.
This check rejects an accidental data leak.
slides.notes: This is an excerpt of the dataset adapter, reformatted across lines. The mask tells training which pixels are likely to belong to the moving object. If an image is reserved for validation, its mask must not influence optimization. The exception makes this error visible immediately. The check does not make view20 a fresh test set: it has already been inspected repeatedly, so it remains a validation camera.
